P1Q1: Whether sacred doctrine is necessary as a science distinct from philosophy, what it studies, and whether it argues from authority, uses metaphors, and admits several senses of Scripture.
P1Q2: Whether God's existence is self-evident or demonstrable; concludes it can be proved by reason through the five ways: motion, causation, contingency, gradation, and design.
P1Q3: Whether God is a body, composed of matter and form, or otherwise composite; concludes God is wholly simple, identical with His own essence and existence.
P1Q4: Whether God is perfect, whether the perfections of all creatures pre-exist eminently in Him, and whether any creature can truly be said to resemble God.
P1Q5: Whether goodness really differs from being, whether every being is good, and how goodness relates to mode, species, order, and final causality.
P1Q6: Whether God is good, the supreme good, essentially good in a way proper to Him alone, and the source of all created goodness.
P1Q7: Whether God is infinite, whether anything besides God can be essentially infinite, and whether an actually infinite magnitude or multitude can exist.
P1Q8: Whether God exists in all things, is everywhere, and is present to creatures by essence, presence, and power in a way unique to Him.
P1Q9: Whether God is altogether immutable, incapable of change in any respect, and whether immutability belongs to God alone among beings.
P1Q10: Defines eternity as the whole and perfect possession of interminable life, asks whether God alone is eternal, and distinguishes eternity from time and aeviternity.
P1Q11: Whether unity adds anything to being, whether one and many are truly opposed, and whether God is one, indeed supremely and uniquely one.
P1Q12: Whether and how the created intellect can see God's essence, requiring a created light of glory, and whether natural reason alone can know God in this life.
P1Q13: Whether names can be applied to God properly or only analogically, and whether "He Who Is" is God's most proper and fitting name.
P1Q14: Treats God's knowledge, asking whether God understands Himself and all other things—including evils, singulars, future contingents, and the infinite—without any discursive reasoning.
P1Q15: Whether there are ideas in the divine mind, whether they are many rather than one, and whether there is an idea for everything God knows.
P1Q16: Whether truth resides properly in the intellect, whether being and truth are convertible terms, and whether God is truth itself, one and immutable.
P1Q17: Whether falsity exists in things themselves, in the senses, or only in the intellect, and how truth and falsity stand as contraries.
P1Q18: Whether life belongs to all natural things, whether life is essentially an operation, and whether life is properly and supremely attributed to God.
P1Q19: Examines whether God possesses will, wills things besides Himself, wills necessarily or freely, and whether the divine will is the cause of all created things.
P1Q20: Whether love exists in God, whether God loves all things that exist, and whether He loves the better things more than the lesser.
P1Q21: Whether justice and mercy can rightly be attributed to God, whether His justice is truth, and how both mercy and justice appear in every divine work.
P1Q22: Whether providence can be attributed to God, whether everything without exception is subject to it, and whether it imposes necessity on the things foreseen.
P1Q23: Treats predestination: whether men are predestined by God, whether God reprobates anyone, and whether the number of the predestined is fixed and certain.
P1Q24: Whether the book of life is the same reality as predestination, whether it concerns only the life of glory, and whether anyone can be blotted out of it.
P1Q25: Whether power belongs to God, whether His power is infinite, whether He is omnipotent, and the limits of omnipotence regarding contradictions and the past.
P1Q26: Whether beatitude belongs to God, whether God constitutes the beatitude of every blessed soul, and how all created beatitude is contained within His own.
P1Q27: Whether there is procession within God, distinguishing the procession of the Word by way of intellect from the procession of Love by way of will.
P1Q28: Whether there are real relations in God distinct from His essence, whether these relations differ from one another, and whether there are exactly four real relations.
P1Q29: Defines "person" and asks whether the term applies fittingly to God, whether it equals hypostasis or subsistence, and whether it signifies relation.
P1Q30: Whether there are several persons in God, whether there are more than three, and whether numerical terms like "three" denote anything real in the Godhead.
P1Q31: Treats the Trinity's unity amid distinction, whether the Son is truly other than the Father, and the proper theological use of exclusive terms like "alone."
P1Q32: Whether the Trinity of persons can be known by unaided natural reason, and whether there are exactly five personal "notions" distinguishing the persons in God.
P1Q33: Whether it belongs to the Father to be the principle without principle, whether "Father" is properly a personal name, and whether unbegottenness is proper to Him.
P1Q34: Whether "Word" functions as a personal name in God, whether it is the Son's proper name, and whether it implies any relation to creatures.
P1Q35: Whether "Image" is used personally rather than essentially in speaking of God, and whether the name Image belongs properly to the Son alone.
P1Q36: Whether "Holy Ghost" is the proper name of one divine person, whether He proceeds from the Son as from the Father, as one single principle.
P1Q37: Whether "Love" is the Holy Ghost's proper personal name, and whether the Father and Son love one another precisely through the Holy Ghost.
P1Q38: Whether "Gift" functions as a personal name in God, and whether Gift is the proper and fitting name of the Holy Ghost specifically.
P1Q39: Whether the divine essence is identical with the person, whether essential names can stand for a person, and how essential attributes are fittingly appropriated to each person.
P1Q40: Whether relation is identical with person in God, whether the persons are distinguished precisely by their relations, and whether properties presuppose the notional acts.
P1Q41: Whether notional acts belong properly to the divine persons, whether they are voluntary, proceed from some principle, and whether several persons can share one act's term.
P1Q42: Whether there is real equality among the divine persons, whether the Son is co-eternal with the Father, and equal to Him in greatness and power.
P1Q43: Whether a divine person can properly be "sent," whether mission is eternal or temporal, and how the visible and invisible missions of Son and Spirit occur.
P1Q44: Whether every being must be created by God, whether primary matter itself is created, and whether God is both the exemplar and final cause of all things.
P1Q45: Defines creation as making something from nothing, asks whether creating belongs to God alone, and whether a trace of the Trinity appears in creatures.
P1Q46: Whether the universe of creatures always existed, whether the world's beginning is an article of faith rather than demonstrable, and whether creation coincided with time's start.
P1Q47: Whether the multitude and distinction of things, and the inequality among them, come from God, and whether only one world exists.
P1Q48: Treats the distinction of good from evil, whether evil is itself a nature, exists as a real privation in things, and how it relates to pain and fault.
P1Q49: Whether good can be the cause of evil, whether the supreme good God is in any sense its cause, and whether one supreme evil causes all evils.
P1Q50: Whether angels are wholly incorporeal, whether they are composed of matter and form, exist in great numbers, differ specifically, and are naturally incorruptible.
P1Q51: Whether angels have bodies naturally united to them, whether they assume bodies at times, and whether they exercise functions of life in those assumed bodies.
P1Q52: Whether an angel occupies a place, whether an angel can be in several places at once, and whether several angels can occupy the same place together.
P1Q53: Whether angels can move locally, whether such movement passes through intermediate space, and whether angelic local movement can occur instantaneously.
P1Q54: Whether an angel's act of understanding is identical with his substance or existence, whether he has active and passive intellect, and possesses only intellectual knowledge.
P1Q55: Whether angels know all things through their own substance or through received species, and whether higher angels understand by fewer, more universal species than lower ones.
P1Q56: Whether an angel knows himself directly, whether one angel knows another, and whether an angel can know God through his own natural principles.
P1Q57: Whether angels know material things, singular things, the future, secret thoughts of the heart, and the hidden mysteries of grace.
P1Q58: Whether an angel's intellect passes from potentiality to act, whether he can understand many things simultaneously, discursively, and possesses "morning" and "evening" knowledge.
P1Q59: Whether angels possess will as distinct from intellect, whether they have genuine free will, and whether irascible and concupiscible appetites exist in them.
P1Q60: Whether angels have natural love and love of choice, love themselves and each other, and love God above self through natural love alone.
P1Q61: Whether angels have a cause of their existence, were produced from eternity, created before the corporeal world, and specifically within the empyrean heaven.
P1Q62: Whether angels were created already in beatitude and grace, needed grace to turn toward God, merited beatitude by a single act, and whether the blessed can still sin.
P1Q63: Whether the evil of sin can affect angels, whether only pride and envy occur among them, and how many angels fell with the highest one.
P1Q64: Whether the demons' intellect is darkened by loss of truth, whether their will is fixed obstinately in evil, whether they suffer sorrow, and where they are punished.
P1Q65: Whether corporeal creatures derive from God, exist for the sake of His goodness, and were produced with the angels serving as intermediaries in their formation.
P1Q66: Whether formless matter preceded formed matter in time, whether all corporeal formless matter was originally uniform, and whether time itself began with formless matter.
P1Q67: Examines whether "light" is used properly of spiritual things, whether light is a body or a quality, and why light's creation is fittingly assigned to the first day.
P1Q68: Treats the second day's work of creation: the making of the firmament, the waters said to exist above it, and whether only one heaven exists.
P1Q69: Treats the third day's work: the fitting gathering together of the waters into seas and the production of plants from the earth.
P1Q70: Treats the fourth day's work: why the heavenly lights were produced then, the reasons assigned for their purpose, and whether they are living beings.
P1Q71: Treats the fifth day's work of creation: the fitting production of fish and birds together from the waters, according to the Genesis account.
P1Q72: Treats the sixth day's work of creation: the production of land animals and finally of man, completing the ordered work of the six days.
P1Q73: Whether the completion of God's works is fittingly ascribed to the seventh day, whether God truly rested, and why that day was blessed and sanctified.
P1Q74: Whether the days of creation are sufficiently enumerated, whether they constitute one day in a real sense, and whether Scripture's wording fittingly expresses the six days' work.
P1Q75: Whether the soul is a body, is subsistent in itself, is identical with man, is composed of matter and form, and is naturally incorruptible.
P1Q76: Whether the intellectual soul is united to the body as its substantial form, whether it is multiplied according to bodies, and whether man has one or several souls.
P1Q77: Whether the soul's essence is identical with its powers, whether it has several distinct powers, and how those powers are ordered and related to the essence.
P1Q78: Distinguishes five genera of the soul's powers—vegetative, sensitive, appetitive, locomotive, and intellective—and the exterior and interior senses within the sensitive part.
P1Q79: Whether intellect is a passive power of the soul, whether an active intellect exists and is one in all men, and distinguishes reason, memory, and conscience.
P1Q80: Whether appetite constitutes a distinct power of the soul beyond apprehension, and whether sensitive and intellectual appetite are genuinely distinct powers.
P1Q81: Whether sensuality is purely appetitive in nature, whether irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers of the sensitive appetite, and whether they obey reason.
P1Q82: Whether the will necessarily desires whatever it wills, whether it ranks higher than intellect, and whether the will in turn can move the intellect.
P1Q83: Whether man possesses free will, whether free will constitutes a distinct appetitive power from the will itself, and how it is properly defined.
P1Q84: Whether the soul knows bodies through the intellect, through innate or separate species, or derives its knowledge from sensible things by way of phantasms.
P1Q85: Whether the intellect understands corporeal things by abstraction from phantasms, whether the universal is known first, and whether the intellect can ever be deceived.
P1Q86: Whether our intellect can know singular material things directly, the infinite, contingent things, and future events through its natural operation.
P1Q87: Whether the intellectual soul knows itself and its own habits through its essence, and whether it knows its own acts and those of the will.
P1Q88: Whether the human soul in its present state can directly understand immaterial substances, and whether God is the very first object known by the human mind.
P1Q89: Whether the soul separated from the body can still understand, know separate substances, know all natural things, singulars, and retain previously acquired knowledge.
P1Q90: Whether the soul was made or is somehow of God's own substance, whether it is produced by creation, immediately by God, and before or with the body.
P1Q91: Whether the first man's body was made from the slime of the earth, produced immediately by God, and given an apt bodily disposition for the soul.
P1Q92: Whether woman should have been made in the first production of things, from man specifically, from his rib, and formed immediately by God Himself.
P1Q93: Whether the image of God exists in man, in irrational creatures, in every human being, and according to the Trinity, the mind, and the soul's acts.
P1Q94: Whether Adam in his first state saw God's essence directly, knew the angels, knew all things, and whether he was capable of being deceived.
P1Q95: Whether the first man was created already in grace, experienced passions, possessed all the virtues, and whether his acts were less meritorious than acts performed now.
P1Q96: Whether Adam held mastership over the animals and all lower creatures, whether men were originally equal, and whether man would have ruled over man.
P1Q97: Whether man in the state of innocence would have been immortal, impassible, needed food, and whether the tree of life would have secured his immortality.
P1Q98: Whether generation of offspring would have occurred in the state of innocence, and whether it would have taken place through bodily coition as it does now.
P1Q99: Whether children in the state of innocence would have had perfect bodily strength immediately after birth, and whether women would still have been born.
P1Q100: Whether children in the state of innocence would have been born already in a state of righteousness, and confirmed unchangeably in that righteousness.
P1Q101: Whether children in the state of innocence would have been born already possessing perfect knowledge and the full, immediate use of reason.
P1Q102: Whether paradise is a real corporeal place fitted to be man's abode, and whether man was created there specifically to dress and keep it.
P1Q103: Whether the world is governed by someone, whether that governance's end lies outside the world, whether one governor suffices, and whether all things are subject to it.
P1Q104: Whether creatures need to be continually kept in being by God, whether He preserves each creature immediately, and whether annihilation of a creature ever occurs.
P1Q105: Whether God can move matter, bodies, the created intellect, and will immediately of Himself, work in every secondary agent, and produce miracles outside nature's order.
P1Q106: Whether one angel can enlighten another or move another angel's will, and whether an inferior angel is ever able to enlighten a superior one.
P1Q107: Whether one angel speaks to another and to God, whether local distance affects such angelic speech, and whether all angels know what one speaks to another.
P1Q108: Whether all angels belong to a single hierarchy, whether several orders exist within it, and how the traditional angelic orders are named and properly ranked.
P1Q109: Whether there is order and precedence among the fallen demons, and whether they retain any enlightenment, being subordinate still to the good angels.
P1Q110: Whether corporeal creatures are governed by angels, whether matter and bodies obey an angel's will and command local motion, and whether angels can work true miracles.
P1Q111: Whether an angel can enlighten a human mind, and whether an angel can change a person's will, imagination, and bodily senses.
P1Q112: Whether angels are sent forth on ministries to men, whether every angel is so sent, assists before God, or belongs to the sent orders.
P1Q113: Whether men are guarded by angels, each person assigned a personal guardian from birth who never abandons him, and whether angels can grieve or contend among themselves.
P1Q114: Whether men are assailed and tempted by demons, whether every sin traces to such temptation, and whether demons are capable of working genuine miracles.
P1Q115: Whether bodies can act as genuine causes, possess seminal powers, and whether heavenly bodies cause earthly effects, human actions, and influence on the demons.
P1Q116: Whether fate truly exists, resides within created things themselves, is unchangeable, and whether absolutely all things are subject to its influence.
P1Q117: Whether one man can teach another or teach the angels, and whether the human soul, especially separated from the body, can move corporeal matter directly.
P1Q118: Whether the sensitive soul is transmitted through the semen, whether the intellectual soul likewise arises from it, or whether all souls were created together at the world's start.
P1Q119: Whether some part of ingested food is truly converted into human nature, and whether human semen is produced specifically from surplus nourishment.
P2Q1: Whether man necessarily acts for an end, whether this is proper to rational nature, whether acts are specified by their end, and whether all men share one last end.
P2Q2: Whether happiness consists in wealth, honors, fame, power, bodily goods, or pleasure, concluding that no created good, however excellent, can fully satisfy man.
P2Q3: Whether happiness is uncreated, essentially an operation of intellect or will, and whether perfect happiness ultimately consists in the direct vision of God's essence.
P2Q4: Whether delight, vision, comprehension, rectitude of will, the body, and the company of friends are all genuinely required for perfect human happiness.
P2Q5: Whether man can actually attain happiness, whether one person can be happier than another, whether it can be lost, and whether it requires grace beyond nature.
P2Q6: Whether human acts are truly voluntary, and whether violence, fear, concupiscence, or ignorance can cause an act to become involuntary.
P2Q7: Whether a circumstance counts as an accident of a human act that theologians must weigh, and which circumstances matter most in moral evaluation.
P2Q8: Whether the will's proper object is good alone, whether volition concerns only the end or also the means, and by what act it wills both together.
P2Q9: Whether the will is moved by the intellect, the sensitive appetite, by itself, by an exterior principle, a heavenly body, or ultimately by God alone.
P2Q10: Whether the will is moved naturally toward some things, whether it is moved of necessity by its object or the lower appetite, or by God as exterior mover.
P2Q11: Whether enjoyment is an act proper to the appetitive power, belongs to rational creatures alone, and concerns only the last end, whether possessed or not.
P2Q12: Whether intention is an act of intellect or will, concerns only the last end, and whether a person can intend two things at the same time.
P2Q13: Whether choice is an act of will or of reason, found in irrational animals, concerns means or sometimes the end, and whether it is exercised freely.
P2Q14: Whether counsel is a genuine inquiry, concerns the end or only the means, regards all our actions, proceeds by analysis, and whether that process is indefinite.
P2Q15: Whether consent is an act of the appetitive or apprehensive power, found in animals, and directed toward the end or toward the means chosen.
P2Q16: Whether use is properly an act of the will, found in irrational animals, extends also to the last end, and whether use precedes choice.
P2Q17: Whether command is an act of reason or of will, and whether it extends to acts of will, reason, sensitive appetite, and even the external bodily members.
P2Q18: Whether human actions can be morally evil, and whether their goodness or evil derives from their object, relevant circumstances, and their ultimate end.
P2Q19: Whether the will's goodness depends on its object, on reason, on the eternal law, and on its conformity to the divine will, even when reason errs.
P2Q20: Whether moral goodness or evil arises first in the interior act of will or in the external act, and how consequences affect an action's moral value.
P2Q21: Whether human acts, insofar as good or evil, are properly called right or sinful, praiseworthy or blameworthy, and meritorious or demeritorious before God.
P2Q22: Whether passion truly exists in the soul, and whether it resides in the appetitive rather than the apprehensive part, chiefly the sensitive appetite.
P2Q23: Whether the passions of the irascible power differ from those of the concupiscible, and how contrariety and specific differences apply among the various passions.
P2Q24: Whether moral good and evil can be found in the passions of the soul, whether every passion is morally evil, and how passion affects an act's goodness.
P2Q25: Whether the irascible passions precede the concupiscible or the reverse, whether love and hope come first, and whether joy, sadness, hope, and fear are the four principal passions.
P2Q26: Whether love resides in the concupiscible power, is itself a passion, is identical with dilection, and divides properly into love of friendship and of concupiscence.
P2Q27: Whether good alone is the cause of love, and whether knowledge, likeness, and other passions of the soul also serve as causes of love.
P2Q28: Whether union, mutual indwelling, ecstasy, zeal, the wounding of the lover, and the origin of all the lover's deeds are true effects of love.
P2Q29: Whether evil is the cause and object of hatred, whether love causes hatred, whether hatred exceeds love in strength, and whether one can hate oneself or truth.
P2Q30: Whether concupiscence belongs solely to the sensitive appetite, is a specific passion, divides into natural and non-natural kinds, and can be infinite.
P2Q31: Whether delight is a passion existing in time, differs from joy, and whether bodily and sensible pleasures exceed spiritual and intellectual pleasures in intensity.
P2Q32: Whether operation, movement, hope, memory, sadness, others' actions, benevolence, likeness, and wonder each serve as genuine causes of pleasure.
P2Q33: Whether expansion, a renewed desire for itself, hindrance of reason's use, and the perfecting of operation are the proper effects of pleasure.
P2Q34: Whether every pleasure is evil, whether every pleasure is good, whether any pleasure is the greatest good, and whether pleasure measures moral good and evil.
P2Q35: Whether pain is a passion of the soul, is the same as sorrow, is contrary to pleasure, and whether outward bodily pain exceeds interior sorrow.
P2Q36: Whether sorrow is caused by loss of a good or the presence of evil, by unfulfilled desire, by longing for unity, or by an irresistible power.
P2Q37: Whether pain deprives a person of the power to learn, burdens the soul, weakens all activity, and harms the body more than other passions do.
P2Q38: Whether pleasure, tears, the sympathy of friends, the contemplation of truth, and sleep or baths each serve as effective remedies against sorrow.
P2Q39: Whether all sorrow is evil, whether sorrow can be a virtuous or useful good, and whether bodily pain ranks as the greatest evil of all.
P2Q40: Whether hope is the same as desire, resides in apprehension or appetite, exists in animals, and how experience, love, and action relate to hope and despair.
P2Q41: Whether fear is a genuine passion of the soul, a special and distinct passion, exists naturally, and how its various species are properly assigned.
P2Q42: Whether the object of fear is good or evil, whether natural evils and the evil of sin can be feared, and what things are most feared.
P2Q43: Whether love and personal defect, such as weakness or a sense of inadequacy, serve as the underlying causes that give rise to the passion of fear.
P2Q44: Whether fear causes bodily contraction, makes one more fit for taking counsel, causes trembling, and generally hinders effective action.
P2Q45: Whether daring is contrary to fear, follows upon hope, arises from some underlying defect, and whether the brave are keener before danger than in the midst of it.
P2Q46: Whether anger is a special passion regarding good or evil, resides in the irascible power, requires an act of reason, and how its species are assigned.
P2Q47: Whether anger's motive is always some injury done against the angry person, whether slight or contempt alone suffices, and how excellence or defect affects anger.
P2Q48: Whether anger causes pleasure, produces fervor of heart above all, hinders the use of reason most, and characteristically causes taciturnity in the angry.
P2Q49: Whether habit is a quality, a distinct species of quality, implies order toward an act, and whether habits are genuinely necessary for human life.
P2Q50: Whether the body, the soul's essence or its powers, the sensitive powers, the intellect, the will, and even angels can serve as subjects of habit.
P2Q51: Whether any habit arises from nature alone, whether habits are caused by repeated acts, by a single act, or infused directly by God.
P2Q52: Whether habits can increase, whether they increase by addition, and whether every single act of a habit actually increases that habit.
P2Q53: Whether a habit can be corrupted, whether it can merely diminish, and whether a habit is corrupted or diminished through simple cessation from acting.
P2Q54: Whether several habits can exist together in one power, whether they are distinguished by their objects, divide into good and bad, and can combine into one.
P2Q55: Whether human virtue is a habit, specifically an operative habit, always a good habit, and whether it is suitably defined as a good quality of the mind.
P2Q56: Whether the subject of virtue is a power of the soul, several powers at once, the intellect, the irascible and concupiscible powers, the senses, or the will.
P2Q57: Distinguishes the intellectual virtues of wisdom, science, understanding, art, and prudence, and identifies the auxiliary virtues annexed to prudence.
P2Q58: Whether every virtue counts as a moral virtue, how moral virtue differs from intellectual virtue, and whether either kind can exist without the other.
P2Q59: Whether moral virtue is itself a passion, is compatible with passion and even sorrow, and whether all moral virtues necessarily concern the passions.
P2Q60: Whether there exists only a single moral virtue, and how the moral virtues differ from one another regarding operations, passions, and their distinct objects.
P2Q61: Whether the cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—are rightly called principal, how they differ, and their division into social, perfecting, and exemplar kinds.
P2Q62: Whether theological virtues exist distinct from intellectual and moral virtues, whether faith, hope, and charity are fittingly named, and their proper order of priority.
P2Q63: Whether virtue arises from nature, is caused through habituation, is infused directly by God, and whether infused and acquired virtue share the same species.
P2Q64: Whether moral, intellectual, and theological virtues all observe a rational or real mean situated between opposite extremes of excess and deficiency.
P2Q65: Whether the moral virtues are mutually interconnected, can exist apart from charity, and whether charity can exist without them or without faith and hope.
P2Q66: Whether one virtue can exceed another in degree, whether the virtues present in one man are all equal, and which virtue ranks greatest overall.
P2Q67: Whether the moral and intellectual virtues, along with faith, hope, and charity, continue to exist after this life or in the state of glory.
P2Q68: Whether the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost differ from the virtues, are necessary for salvation, are habits, remain connected, and persist in heaven.
P2Q69: Whether the eight beatitudes differ from the virtues and gifts, refer strictly to this present life, and are suitably enumerated along with their fitting rewards.
P2Q70: Whether the fruits of the Holy Ghost that Paul enumerates are themselves acts, differ from the beatitudes, and stand opposed to the works of the flesh.
P2Q71: Whether vice stands contrary to virtue and to nature itself, whether vice exceeds a single vicious act in evil, and defines sin as contrary to eternal law.
P2Q72: Whether sins differ in species by their objects, causes, or circumstances, and how sin divides into spiritual versus carnal, and commission versus omission.
P2Q73: Whether all sins are mutually connected and equal in gravity, and what factors—object, cause, circumstance, or resulting harm—make one sin graver than another.
P2Q74: Whether the will, the sensuality, or the reason serves as the proper subject of sin, and whether mortal or venial sin can reside in each.
P2Q75: Whether sin possesses an internal cause within the sinner and an external cause outside him, and whether one sin can itself become the cause of another.
P2Q76: Whether ignorance can cause sin, whether ignorance is itself sinful, and whether it excuses from sin entirely or merely diminishes its guilt.
P2Q77: Whether passion can move the will against reason's own judgment, causing sins of weakness, and whether passion excuses from or merely mitigates mortal sin.
P2Q78: Whether sinning through deliberate malice relates to sinning from settled habit, and whether it is graver than sinning merely through passion.
P2Q79: Whether God can be called a cause of sin or of spiritual blindness and hardness of heart, and whether these ultimately serve the sinner's own salvation.
P2Q80: Whether the devil directly causes human sin, can instigate it internally, can compel a person to sin of necessity, or whether all sin stems from his suggestion.
P2Q81: Whether Adam's original sin, and possibly later ancestral sins, are transmitted by way of origin to all his human descendants without exception.
P2Q82: Whether original sin is properly a habit, whether it consists essentially in concupiscence, and whether it is present equally in every person who inherits it.
P2Q83: Whether original sin resides more properly in the flesh or in the soul, and whether it infects the will before infecting the soul's other powers.
P2Q84: Whether covetousness or pride functions as the root of every sin, and whether the traditional seven capital vices are suitably and completely enumerated.
P2Q85: Whether sin diminishes, or could entirely destroy, the good of human nature, and how weakness, ignorance, malice, concupiscence, and death all result from sin.
P2Q86: Whether sin causes a real stain upon the soul, and whether that stain persists in the soul even after the sinful act itself has ceased.
P2Q87: Whether the debt of punishment is itself an effect of sin, whether it can be eternal in duration, and whether one can justly be punished for another's sin.
P2Q88: Whether venial sin differs generically from mortal sin, whether it disposes toward mortal sin, and whether circumstances can turn a venial sin mortal or vice versa.
P2Q89: Whether venial sin still stains the soul, could have occurred in the state of innocence or among angels, and can coexist with original sin alone.
P2Q90: Whether law pertains essentially to reason, is always ordered to the common good, can be made by any private person, and requires public promulgation.
P2Q91: Whether there exists an eternal law, a natural law within us, human law, and divine law, including a distinct "law of the fomes" of concupiscence.
P2Q92: Whether an effect of law is to make its subjects genuinely good, and what proper acts—commanding, forbidding, permitting, punishing—belong to law as such.
P2Q93: Whether the eternal law is God's sovereign governing plan, known in some way to all, the source from which every other law is derived and binding.
P2Q94: Whether natural law is a habit, contains one precept or many, prescribes every act of virtue, remains the same in all men, and whether it can change.
P2Q95: Whether human laws were usefully devised by men, whether every human law derives from natural law, and whether Isidore's descriptions of positive law hold true.
P2Q96: Whether human law should target the whole community, repress every vice, prescribe every virtuous act, bind in conscience, and whether all persons are subject to it.
P2Q97: Whether human law can rightly be changed, should always change when something better appears, whether custom can gain the force of law, and whether rulers may dispense from it.
P2Q98: Whether the Old Law was good, truly given by God through the angels, intended for the Jews alone, binding on all, and fittingly given in the time of Moses.
P2Q99: Whether the Old Law contains a single precept or many, comprising moral, ceremonial, and judicial precepts, and whether it used temporal rewards to induce obedience.
P2Q100: Whether the Old Law's moral precepts belong essentially to the natural law, cover all acts of virtue, reduce to the Decalogue, and whether they justified man.
P2Q101: Whether the ceremonial precepts concern the worship of God, are essentially figurative, why so many were needed, and how they divide into sacrifices, sacred things, sacraments, observances.
P2Q102: Whether the ceremonial precepts had both literal and figurative causes, assigning specific reasons for the sacrifices, holy things, sacraments, and observances of the Old Law.
P2Q103: Whether the ceremonies of the Old Law existed before the Law itself, once had power to justify, ceased entirely at Christ's coming, and became sinful to observe afterward.
P2Q104: Whether the judicial precepts directed man's relations toward his neighbor, were figurative in meaning, bind perpetually, and how they may be properly classified.
P2Q105: Whether the Old Law's judicial precepts were fittingly framed regarding civil rulers, relations between citizens, treatment of foreigners, and members of the household.
P2Q106: Whether the New Law of the Gospel is essentially a written law, whether it justifies, should have existed from the world's beginning, and will endure until the end.
P2Q107: Whether the New Law is genuinely distinct from the Old Law while fulfilling it, is contained within it, and is more or less burdensome to observe.
P2Q108: Whether the New Law prescribes or prohibits particular external acts, sufficiently orders both interior and exterior actions, and fittingly proposes counsels beyond strict precepts.
P2Q109: Whether man without grace can know truth, will or do any good, love God above all things, fulfill the commandments, merit eternal life, or avoid sin entirely.
P2Q110: Whether grace implies something real in the soul, is properly a quality, differs essentially from virtue, and resides in the soul's essence or in its powers.
P2Q111: Whether grace divides into sanctifying and gratuitous grace, operating and cooperating grace, prevenient and subsequent grace, and how gratuitous grace compares to sanctifying grace.
P2Q112: Whether God alone causes grace in the soul, whether human preparation is required, whether grace varies in degree among persons, and whether one can know he possesses it.
P2Q113: Whether the justification of the ungodly consists in remission of sin, requires infused grace, a movement of free will and faith, and whether it happens instantaneously as God's greatest work.
P2Q114: Whether man can truly merit anything from God, merit eternal life condignly only in grace, merit the first grace for himself or others, merit restoration, or temporal goods.
